QuantitativeFinding: Net route time: Baseline 67.06 s, Tsunami 48.66 s, and Minimap 41.01 s. Both planned one-sided contrasts versus Baseline were p<.001 (Holm adjusted).
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Neither long-range technique was preferred for every short-range or constrained task.
Interpretation: Scale-dependent accounts converge with large long-range net-time advantages for both extended techniques.
EvidentialBoundary: The result does not establish one universally optimal method; effects depended on the tested tasks and routes.

QuantitativeFinding: Relative to Baseline, teleport-count incidence-rate ratios were 0.191 for Minimap and 0.369 for Tsunami; path-efficiency ratios were 1.032 and 0.959, respectively (all Holm-adjusted p<.001).
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Time, action count, and spatial economy did not rank methods identically.
Interpretation: The two long-range techniques reduced interaction effort differently, while Minimap and Tsunami showed opposite path-efficiency directions relative to Baseline.
EvidentialBoundary: These outcomes are exploratory and describe the evaluated implementations rather than intrinsic technique properties.

QuantitativeFinding: Method-by-route likelihood-ratio tests were significant for net time, chi-square(4)=32.86, p<.001, and total time, chi-square(4)=28.00, p<.001.
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Route-level variation did not identify a single geometric cause.
Interpretation: Route layout moderated method effects, supporting the qualitative account of context-dependent practical fit.
EvidentialBoundary: An interaction identifies variation but does not by itself establish which route feature caused it.

QuantitativeFinding: Perceived spatial awareness was higher for Tsunami than Minimap (means 4.62 vs 3.06; difference 1.56, 95% CI [1.11, 2.02], p<.001; confirmatory). Perceived environmental continuity was also higher (means 4.4048 vs 2.9048; difference 1.5000, 95% CI [0.8109, 2.1891], p<.001; exploratory).
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Minimap sometimes provided a useful global overview; Tsunami did not always help when landmarks or destinations were unclear.
Interpretation: Participant accounts contextualize the subjective rating differences in perceptual information available during locomotion.
EvidentialBoundary: These ratings concern perceived awareness and continuity, not acquired spatial knowledge; some map-frame problems were implementation-conditioned.

QuantitativeFinding: Event-level models found lower adjusted landing-to-confirmation latency for Tsunami than Minimap (2.05 vs 2.85 s; difference -0.80 s, p<.001) and lower head rotation (4.55 vs 26.22 degrees; difference -21.67 degrees, p<.001).
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Movement strategies varied and did not directly index what participants learned about the environment.
Interpretation: Behavior during landing confirmation complements subjective and interview evidence about technique-specific interaction strategies.
EvidentialBoundary: Head movement is a behavioral measure, not a direct measure of visual attention, spatial cognition, or awareness.

QuantitativeFinding: During landing-to-confirmation, Tsunami-to-Minimap adjusted (outcome+1) ratios were 0.354 for absolute yaw (95% CI [0.317, 0.396]) and 0.180 for absolute pitch (95% CI [0.164, 0.198]); both Holm-adjusted p<.001.
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: The measures isolate movement components but not participants' cognitive representation.
Interpretation: The decomposition supports phase-specific behavioral differences between interfaces.
EvidentialBoundary: Yaw and pitch are movement components within a defined interval and must not be interpreted as spatial cognition.

QuantitativeFinding: For direct-hit long-range trials, adjusted Tsunami-minus-Minimap landing-error differences were 1.22 m at 200-350 m and 1.69 m at 350-500 m (both Holm-adjusted p<.001). The continuous method-by-distance interaction was not significant (p=.250).
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Participants distinguished the technique concept from joystick release, filtering, map controls, and UI placement.
Interpretation: The tested Minimap implementation produced lower direct-hit landing error; qualitative evidence identifies plausible implementation-conditioned contributors.
EvidentialBoundary: The non-significant interaction is not evidence of equivalence, and the measured difference must not be generalized to all implementations.

QuantitativeFinding: For complete sequential checkpoint episodes, adjusted first-landing errors were Tsunami 7.96 vs Minimap 1.79 m at 200-350 m and 18.27 vs 2.57 m at 350-500 m (both Holm-adjusted p<.001); the continuous method-by-distance interaction was p=.001.
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Alternative controls and smoothing were proposed but not experimentally evaluated.
Interpretation: Reports of overshoot and corrective action contextualize the sequential-approach pattern, especially at greater distance.
EvidentialBoundary: Control remapping and filtering remain design implications, not demonstrated causal fixes.

QuantitativeFinding: Across repeated post-confirmation events, end-to-start (outcome+1) ratios were 0.760 for Minimap and 0.816 for Tsunami latency, and 0.662 and 0.575 for head rotation (all within-method p<.001). Method-by-progress interactions were non-significant for latency (p=.101) and head rotation (p=.389).
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Some participants remained uncomfortable or preferred familiar Baseline control.
Interpretation: Reported acclimatization converges with reduced interaction and movement demands during repeated use.
EvidentialBoundary: Exploratory change does not demonstrate universal mastery or different learning rates between methods.

QuantitativeFinding: Minimap had lower net time than Tsunami (41.01 vs 48.66 s, p<.001; exploratory), whereas total times did not differ (60.70 vs 61.95 s, p=.603; exploratory). RAW-TLX favored Tsunami (17.78 vs 21.15; one-sided p=.029; confirmatory). Usability favored Tsunami by 0.92 points (p<.001; exploratory), and preference ranks favored Tsunami over Minimap by 0.74 points (Holm-adjusted p=.002; exploratory).
ContradictoryOrDivergentCases: Minimap's lower preference did not negate its active-traversal speed and tested precision advantages.
Interpretation: Instrumental speed did not map directly onto workload, usability ratings, or preference; adoption reflected multiple criteria.
EvidentialBoundary: Preference is not general usability. The workload confidence interval for the paired mean difference slightly included zero despite the significant planned rank test.

QuantitativeFinding: Mean CSQ-VR changes were Baseline 0.33, Tsunami 0.29, and Minimap 0.17. The planned Tsunami-versus-Baseline one-sided test was non-significant (p=.652); exploratory Minimap contrasts were also non-significant after Holm correction.
Interpretation: Sparse symptom reports are compatible with small average changes and no detected method-specific difference.
EvidentialBoundary: Non-significance does not establish equivalence or absence of individual cybersickness.
